narrative.title: Why Kelsey?
narrative.body:
I have always been drawn to work where preparation, purpose, and people intersect. My career has given me a unique perspective on how decisions are made, from analyzing complex financial information to learning how to respond calmly and effectively in moments that matter most. Those experiences have shaped the way I approach healthcare: I am naturally curious, highly driven, and motivated by the opportunity to take something complicated and make it meaningful to the person standing in front of me.

What ultimately draws me to healthcare and medical sales is the human side of the work. Behind every number, treatment decision, or business objective is a physician trying to provide the best care, a healthcare organization trying to solve a difficult problem, or a patient whose life may be changed by the right decision. I want to be the person who earns the trust to help move those decisions forward. I bring analytical discipline and a strong business mindset, but I lead with empathy, preparation, and genuine service. I want to build relationships that last beyond a single conversation and become someone my customers know they can rely on.

I am ambitious, but my ambition has never been simply about achieving the next title or number. I want to build a career I can be proud of, one where I am constantly learning, surrounded by people who challenge me, and able to see the tangible impact of my work. I bring the persistence of someone who does not give up easily, the confidence to walk into a room and contribute, and the humility to listen before assuming I have the answer. For me, success means becoming the kind of partner people trust when the decision matters.

startStories.title: Account Retention and Client Trust
startStories.teaser: At Goldman Sachs I held a book of roughly 20 multi-million dollar lending accounts at 100% retention with zero escalations.
startStories.body:
I managed a portfolio of institutional clients across multi million dollar syndicated loan accounts. The contracts behind those loans ran 100 to 250 pages of dense legal language, and a rate change buried at one specific point in the contract could not be missed. I learned to read those contracts front to back so I'd catch a discrepancy before it ever reached a client.

When clients had questions I answered in plain terms, not legal speak, because their trust in me depended on actually understanding what I told them. I kept every deadline I gave a client, including working from a plane on Christmas Eve once, because the commitment mattered more than the inconvenience. When teammates were out I picked up their accounts too, so no client ever felt a gap in service.

I was the face of Goldman to those clients. That meant white glove service and 100% accuracy at the same time, no exceptions. I kept every account in my book and never had a single issue escalate.

That role taught me accuracy and warmth aren't a tradeoff. A client has to trust you're never wrong on the details and that you value their time as much as your own deadlines. That's exactly what a physician expects from a rep.

startStories.title: Clinical Credibility
startStories.teaser: I finished my EMT program in the top 5% of my class and spent my rotations in emergency, surgical, and in-transit care.
startStories.body:
I did not come to medical sales from a classroom. I finished the UT Dallas EMT program in the top 5% of my cohort and did clinical rotations in emergency, surgical, and in-transit environments, which is where the training stopped being theoretical.

One night I was three months in, about 2am during a 12 hour overnight shift. My mentor pulled me mid task and told me to follow two nurses immediately. We ran to the rooftop helipad to receive an emergency air transport. The nurses taught me the protocol on the way up. We received the patient and moved him through the hospital into the trauma bay.

The surgeon came in. A couple of EMT students were in the room. He barked a command to cut the patient's clothes off with shears. I stepped forward immediately and started cutting while the surgeon performed what I later identified as an emergency tracheotomy. The nurses looked over their shoulders and told the other students who had frozen to follow my lead.

That kind of experience is why I can hold a real conversation with a physician about clinical realities instead of reciting a detail aid. I know what a bad night looks like on their side of the desk, I know how a handoff actually works, and I know what it costs them when a product adds a step.

You do not rise to the occasion. You fall to your level of preparation. That is true in a trauma bay and it is true walking into an office where you have eight minutes.

startStories.title: Business Acumen and Data-Driven Insight
startStories.teaser: I found a $2M revenue opportunity nobody assigned me at Vivint, and built a national marketing heat map across 41,000 ZIP codes at 1-800 Contacts.
startStories.body:
I joined Vivint without knowing SQL or the business intelligence tools the team ran on. I learned both and delivered executive-level reporting within 9 days of starting. The dashboards I built were used by the COO and 6 department leaders, and the numbers in them were presented on C-suite quarterly earnings calls.

Once I was in the data every day I started noticing patterns nobody had asked me to look for. I identified 7 to 8 operational inefficiencies across field and operations performance. Together they added up to roughly $2M in revenue opportunity. I built the case, sized it, presented it to senior leadership, and they reallocated resources based on it.

Earlier, as a financial analyst intern at 1-800 Contacts, my assignment was recurring executive reporting for a direct-to-consumer medical device retailer. The reports were accurate but they did not show leadership where advertising money was actually working. I built a nationwide marketing performance heat map covering more than 41,000 U.S. ZIP codes so spend could be seen against customer acquisition geographically. It exposed inefficient spend and identified markets worth growing. I then ran an independent 50-state analysis outside my assigned responsibilities using a visualization approach the team had not used before, and they adopted it.

A territory is a data set. Most reps report on theirs. I have spent my career finding the thing inside the numbers that nobody asked about, sizing it, and getting decision makers to act on it.

startStories.title: Territory Building and Bilingual Reach
startStories.teaser: I inherited a Spanish-speaking territory across three states that previous reps had written off, and built it into one of the strongest in the district.
startStories.body:
My job was to find people willing to join our organization. Cold calling strangers rarely worked, warm referrals did. Most members weren't reps like me, they were local families who met multiple times a week. In each area, one key stakeholder connected reps to those members. Mine had shut out every rep before me, and the territory's numbers had suffered for it.

I didn't push. My companion and I got to know his wife first, no agenda, just showing up over time. Eventually she mentioned he missed playing pickup soccer. That was my opening. We organized a game. He came. We kept it going. He went from closed off to actively referring members and trusting us with his network.

That territory became one of the strongest in the district. More than half of our new commitments came through referrals rather than cold outreach.

What that taught me is a no isn't the end, it just means you haven't found the right angle yet. Trust can't be rushed. That's exactly what it takes with a physician who's already said no to reps before.

startStories.title: Leadership, Coaching, and Training
startStories.teaser: I have led 100+ volunteer advocates, coached underperforming teammates at Goldman, and trained a 10-person analytics team on tools I introduced.
startStories.body:
As Executive Director of the BYU chapter of CASA, I directed a 5-member executive team overseeing more than 100 volunteer advocates supporting children involved in the court system. The roster looked healthy on paper, but a meaningful share of advocates never finished certification, which meant they could not be assigned to a child. I focused the leadership team on completion rather than recruitment and drove up the share of active, fully certified advocates. The role also meant working directly with judges, attorneys, families, and community partners, each with different priorities and no obligation to make my job easier.

At Goldman Sachs I mentored an intern and two underperforming teammates through individualized coaching. Coaching someone who is struggling is different from managing someone who is not. It requires figuring out whether the gap is knowledge, confidence, or process before you try to fix anything.

At 1-800 Contacts I trained the full 10-person analytics team on Excel visualization tools I had introduced, which meant teaching people who had been there longer than me without making it feel that way.

In every one of those, the work was the same. Find the actual constraint, coach the person through the step they have been avoiding, and measure the outcome instead of the activity.

startStories.title: End-to-End Program Ownership
startStories.teaser: I built a school soccer program from nothing, and when demand outran the roster cap I restructured it instead of turning families away.
startStories.body:
As PK3 Outreach Co-Chair at Meadowbrook School, I own a program end to end. That means recruiting, logistics, communication with families, coordination with the school, and the results.

I built a soccer program from the ground up. Registration outran the league's roster limit almost immediately. Rather than cutting families, I restructured the program into two full teams of 12 so every child who signed up got to play, and coordinated the scheduling, staffing, and communication that made two teams workable instead of one.

Running outreach for the grade also means being the person families actually talk to. Participation depends on whether people trust the person asking.

Nobody hands you a playbook for a program that does not exist yet. You define what success looks like, build the thing, adjust when reality does not match the plan, and stay accountable for the outcome. That is what owning a territory is.
